extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, writers, and public speakers (early 18th-century periodical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, prescriptive literary essays offering norms for taste, oratory, translation, and description — guidance for cultivating fine taste, effective gesture and voice, use of music in worship/drama, and vivid visual imagination. Aimed at readers and practitioners seeking to improve writing and public speaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of music in religious worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Musick, when thus applied, raises noble Hints in the Mind of the Hearer, and fills it with great Conceptions. It strengthens Devotion, and advances Praise into Rapture. It lengthens out every Act of Worship, and produces more lasting and permanent Impressions in the Mind, than those which accompany any transient Form of Words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply vocal and instrumental music in religious services to purify and exalt passions, to give thoughts a proper turn, and to cherish divine impulses; set sacred words to music (as ancient practice) so that works consecrated to the tabernacle also serve as national entertainment and devotion. Example from antiquity: choral hymns surrounding a deity. Implicit norm: musical worship should produce lasting impressions rather than transient effects of spoken words alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the chorus in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The first Original of the Drama was a Religious Worship consisting only of a Chorus, which was nothing else but an Hymn to a Deity. ... in Tragedies the Chorus so far remembered its first Office, as to brand every thing that was vicious, and recommend every thing that was laudable, to intercede with Heaven for the Innocent, and to implore its Vengeance on the Criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing a chorus (or analogous collective voice), use it to mark moral judgement: condemn vice, recommend virtue, and serve as a moral/explanatory commentator that connects the action to religious or civic concerns. This historic role is offered as a model for how dramatic devices may instruct and mediate ethical sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of solitude and public life
rubrics_metrics.description: Methinks most of the Philosophers and Moralists have run too much into Extreams, in praising entirely either Solitude or publick Life; in the former Men generally grow useless by too much Rest, and in the latter are destroyed by too much Precipitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a mixed state: combine retirement and public usefulness (like gentle streams that glide through lonely vales yet visit populous towns). Avoid extremes — excessive solitude leads to uselessness, excessive public activity to ruin. Note: some people are naturally suited to solitude and should not be forced into public display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of poetry: preserve natural images and emotional arc
rubrics_metrics.description: The Circumstances which successively present themselves to him in his Way, are, I believe you will think, naturally interwoven. The Anxiety of Absence, the Gloominess of the Roads, and his Resolution of frequenting only those, ... the Dissatisfaction he expresses even at the greatest Swiftness ... and his joyful Surprize at an unexpected Sight of his Mistress ... seems beautifully described in the Original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In translating lyric or narrative poetry aim to preserve the natural interweaving of circumstances and the emotional progression (anxiety, gloom, impatience, surprise, joy). If exact images are lost, a translation may still serve as a substitute when the original author cannot supply a version, but the translator should endeavour to retain the original's rural images and affective sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory: study and deploy gesture and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is certain that proper Gestures and vehement Exertions of the Voice cannot be too much studied by a publick Orator. They are a kind of Comment to what he utters, and enforce every thing he says, with weak Hearers, better than the strongest Argument he can make use of. They keep the Audience awake, and fix their Attention to what is delivered to them, at the same time that they shew the Speaker is in earnest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public speakers should train expressive gesture and vocal force to reinforce arguments, engage attention, and show earnestness. Study gestures as an accompaniment to speech; used well they serve as commentary and emotional emphasis. Examples from Greek and Latin orators show the powerful effect of action combined with rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory anti-patterns: avoid ridiculous gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often nothing more ridiculous than the Gestures of an English Speaker; you see some of them running their Hands into their Pockets ... others looking with great Attention on a piece of Paper that has nothing written in it; ... turning his Hat in his Hands, moulding it into several different Cocks, examining sometimes the Lining of it, and sometimes the Button ... a Counsellor who never pleaded without a Piece of Pack-thread in his Hand ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mannerisms that distract or undermine authority: hands in pockets, purposeless fiddling with hats or objects, staring at blank papers, or any habitual prop (e.g., pack-thread) that becomes the 'thread of his discourse.' Either dispense with gestures entirely (if that suits the national style) or restrict oneself to gestures that are graceful and expressive rather than comic or fussy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fine taste in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: I think I may define it to be that Faculty of the Soul, which discerns the Beauties of an Author with Pleasure, and the Imperfections with Dislike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine taste is an internal faculty: a reader should feel extraordinary delight at celebrated works and recoil at defects. Test your taste by reading canonical authors of antiquity and approved moderns — lack of pleasurable response suggests deficiency of taste, not of the author. Cultivate sensitivity to subtle perfections and blemishes in style and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernment of specifick qualities in authors
rubrics_metrics.description: He should ... observe, whether he tastes the distinguishing Perfections, or ... the Specifick Qualities of the Author whom he peruses; whether he is particularly pleased with Livy for his Manner of telling a Story, with Sallust for his entering into those internal Principles of Action ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person of fine taste distinguishes author-specific strengths (manner, insight into motives, handling of outward motives). Compare how the same thought strikes you in a great writer versus an ordinary one — this contrast reveals the quality of presentation. Practice identifying those particularities as a way to refine taste and imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to cultivate and improve fine taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The most natural Method for this Purpose is to be conversant among the Writings of the most Polite Authors. Conversation with Men of a Polite Genius is another Method ... It is likewise necessary for a Man who would form to himself a finished Taste of good Writing, to be well versed in the Works of the best Criticks both Ancient and Modern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately read celebrated works of antiquity and approved moderns; converse with accomplished, polite minds to gain alternative perspectives; study leading critics who go beyond mechanical rules and enter the spirit of fine writing. Practical consequence: immersion, dialogue, and critical study together cultivate taste; writers often flourish in contemporaneous groups of geniuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject ephemeral 'Gothic' taste: avoid forced conceits and empty epigrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Our general Taste in England is for Epigram, Turns of Wit, and forced Conceits, which have no manner of Influence, either for the bettering or enlarging the Mind ... I have endeavoured in several of my Speculations to banish this Gothic Taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid valuing clever but shallow verbal effects (epigrams, forced conceits) that do not enlarge or improve the reader's mind. Prefer natural simplicity of thought and expressions that genuinely affect the imagination and understanding. Critical stance: detect and eschew these false kinds admired by fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual description to excite the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Sight is the most perfect and most delightful of all our Senses. ... It is this Sense which furnishes the Imagination with its Ideas; so that by the Pleasures of the Imagination or Fancy ... I here mean such as arise from visible Objects, either when we have them actually in our View, or when we call up their Ideas in our Minds by Paintings, Statues, Descriptions, or any the like Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce pleasures of the imagination, employ visible detail and imagery — actual sight, or the evocation of sight through painting, sculpture, or descriptive writing. Ground imaginative pleasures in well-rendered visual objects so readers' minds receive large, varied ideas and sustained enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and management of passions in character and moral writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The strange and absurd Variety that is so apparent in Men's Actions, shews plainly they can never proceed immediately from Reason; ... The Passions will never be accepted as an Excuse for complying with them, they were designed for Subjection ... The Understanding being of its self too slow and lazy to exert it self into Action, its necessary it should be put in Motion by the gentle Gales of the Passions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting human nature or instructing moral behaviour, treat passions as the principles of action: show their causes and effects, keep them under the guidance of reason rather than suppressing them entirely, and maintain an appropriate proportion between reason and passion (strong geniuses tend to have strong passions). In literary characterization, preserve passions' vigor but show their governance by reason; avoid portraying characters as passionless or irrationally driven.
